name: nutrition-tracker
status: approved by Robert 2026-11-01, and implemented. Four revisions since: the days table was dropped the same day - a day is the date on an entry, not a row of its own - on 2026-11-02 the foods unit list gained the gram basis (2 -> 3), accounts became real: email, telegram id and a stored password hash (3 -> 4), and pairing codes arrived so a chat can be bound to an account (4 -> 5), and a profile per account arrived so calorie and protein targets can be worked out from the person (6 -> 7, Part 12: an additive table, nothing existing touched).

connection_pragmas.why: SQLite defaults it OFF, and every delete guard in this schema is a foreign key. Without this line the storage-level guard from R11 does not exist.
One process writes, but a request can arrive while a write is in flight. Waiting beats an immediate SQLITE_BUSY.

tables.name: users
tables.purpose: One row per person whose log this is. Every other table carries a user_id, which is how R2 holds. Registration (R3, R24) adds rows here, not tables.

columns.name: id
columns.notes: Generated ('user-<12 hex>') for a registered account; the seed's is 'user'. Opaque on purpose: a username is something a person may want to change and a primary key is not.

columns.name: username
columns.notes: What a person signs in with. Unique by column constraint.

columns.name: email
columns.notes: R3 asks for one. Unique by index, and many NULLs are allowed, so an account without one is a normal account - what the email is *for* is D17, still open.

columns.name: telegram_id
columns.notes: R3 asks for one. Digits. This is what R26 will bind a chat to, and it is stored as text because it is an identifier, not a number to do arithmetic on.

columns.name: password_hash
columns.notes: pbkdf2_sha256$iterations$salt$digest (see app/passwords.py). Never returned by a route. Nullable so a row written before registration existed is still a valid row, and a null one fails closed: nobody signs in with it.

tables.name: telegram_codes
tables.purpose: A one-time code that binds a chat to an account (R26, D18): the app shows it, the chat redeems it. Stored rather than signed so that it can be spent - a code that keeps working after it has been used is one somebody else can use.

columns.name: code
columns.notes: Primary key: six characters, no I/L/O/0/1, uppercased before it is stored or looked up.

columns.name: user_id
columns.notes: The account the code was minted for. The chat never chooses this.

columns.name: expires
columns.notes: 15 minutes from minting. Fixed-width UTC, so it compares correctly as a string.

columns.name: used
columns.notes: Spent on redemption, and every other code the account held is spent with it.

tables.name: profiles
tables.purpose: What the targets are worked out from (Part 12, R38-R46): one row per account, inputs only. No target is stored (R42) - a target derived from the weight goes stale the day the weight changes - so the two overrides are the person's own figures, which are inputs too. An account with no row is a legitimate state and sees the fixed targets (R38). Private to the account, and reachable only from a signed-in browser, not by the bot (R41, R53).

columns.name: user_id
columns.notes: Primary key, so a second profile for one account cannot exist. RESTRICT: leaving an account (Part 10 step 4) must remove the profile first.

columns.name: display_name
columns.notes: What the app calls the person. Not the username, which is a login.

columns.name: sex
columns.notes: The calorie equation has one constant for each. Used for that and for the calorie floor, nothing else.

columns.name: birth_date
columns.notes: A date, not an age: an age is derived and goes stale. The 18 to 100 limit is enforced by the route, because it depends on today's date, which a CHECK cannot know.

columns.name: height_cm
columns.notes: Always metric. The units setting changes what the form shows, not what is stored.

columns.name: weight_kg
columns.notes: Always metric.

columns.name: weight_on
columns.notes: When the weight was set. Written by the server, and kept when a save does not change the weight, so the Day view can say what a target rests on (R48).

columns.name: units
columns.notes: A display preference only.

columns.name: kcal_override
columns.notes: The person's own calorie target. It wins over the computed one, and the calorie floor does not apply to it (R46, D28).

columns.name: protein_override
columns.notes: The person's own protein target. Independent of the calorie override.

tables.name: foods
tables.purpose: A food record and the macros one unit of it contributes, matching the frontend's Food type exactly.

columns.name: id
columns.notes: A slug for seeded rows ('hummus'), a generated id for new ones.

columns.name: unit
columns.check: one of the eight units in the app, including `g`, the gram basis

columns.name: calories
columns.notes: Per one unit. REAL because quantities are fractional.

columns.name: source
columns.notes: Where the figures came from: typed by the person, or looked up in USDA FoodData Central (D20). Every food that existed before version 6 reads as typed, which is true of all of them.

columns.name: source_id
columns.notes: USDA's own id (fdcId) for a looked-up food, so a figure can be traced to its origin. Null for a typed food.

tables.not_constrained: No unique constraint on (user_id, name): the app allows two foods with the same name, and a constraint the UI does not enforce would fail a save that looked fine.

tables.name: meals
tables.purpose: A named group of foods, e.g. 'Typical breakfast'. The name is the whole record; the contents live in meal_foods.

tables.name: meal_foods
tables.purpose: Which foods a meal is made of, and how much of each.
tables.not_constrained: No unique (meal_id, food_id): the meal builder lets the same food be added twice, and forbidding it here would reject a form that the UI accepted.

tables.name: entries
tables.purpose: One thing logged into one section of one date: a food with a quantity, or a whole meal. This is the only table the frontend's LogEntry maps to. It carries its own date and its own user, so a day of the log is a query over this table rather than a row that had to exist first.

columns.name: user_id
columns.notes: The entry records whose log it is directly, so every read can be scoped without a join and the isolation rule from R2 is a column rather than a path through two tables.

columns.name: date
columns.notes: Validated with strftime, which normalises an impossible date like 2026-02-31 and so fails the check. The comparison is IS rather than = on purpose: strftime returns NULL for a string it cannot parse, and SQLite treats a CHECK that evaluates to NULL as passing, so = would let a malformed date through. Verified by running it.

columns.name: quantity
columns.notes: Set for a food entry, NULL for a meal entry - the app logs a meal as a whole, with no multiplier.

checks.rule: (food_id IS NOT NULL) + (meal_id IS NOT NULL) = 1
checks.why: An entry is a food or a meal, never both and never neither.
A quantity belongs to a food entry only.

indexes.name: entries_by_user_date
indexes.notes: Every day view is this pair.

tables.ordering: Entries come back in insertion order (SQLite's implicit rowid). No position column: the app never reorders an entry, only adds and removes.

tables.name: meta
tables.purpose: One row recording the schema version, so a database file written by a different version of this schema is refused with a clear message instead of misbehaving.

ddl:
CREATE TABLE users (
    id            TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    username      TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    email         TEXT,
    telegram_id   TEXT,
    password_hash TEXT
)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS users_by_email ON users (email)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS users_by_telegram ON users (telegram_id)

CREATE TABLE telegram_codes (
    code    TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    expires TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ', expires) IS expires),
    used    INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (used IN (0, 1))
)

CREATE TABLE profiles (
    user_id          TEXT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    display_name     TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (length(display_name) BETWEEN 1 AND 40),
    sex              TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (sex IN ('female', 'male')),
    birth_date       TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (date(birth_date) IS birth_date),
    height_cm        REAL NOT NULL CHECK (height_cm BETWEEN 120 AND 230),
    weight_kg        REAL NOT NULL CHECK (weight_kg BETWEEN 30 AND 300),
    weight_on        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (date(weight_on) IS weight_on),
    activity         TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (activity IN ('sedentary', 'light', 'moderate', 'active', 'very_active')),
    goal             TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (goal IN ('lose', 'maintain', 'gain')),
    units            TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'metric' CHECK (units IN ('metric', 'imperial')),
    kcal_override    INTEGER CHECK (kcal_override IS NULL OR kcal_override BETWEEN 800 AND 6000),
    protein_override INTEGER CHECK (protein_override IS NULL OR protein_override BETWEEN 20 AND 400)
)

CREATE TABLE foods (
    id       TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id  TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    name     TEXT NOT NULL,
    unit     TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (unit IN ('cup', 'tbsp', 'tsp', 'oz', 'piece', 'slice', 'scoop', 'g')),
    calories REAL NOT NULL CHECK (calories >= 0),
    protein  REAL NOT NULL CHECK (protein >= 0),
    carbs    REAL NOT NULL CHECK (carbs >= 0),
    fat      REAL NOT NULL CHECK (fat >= 0),
    source    TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'typed' CHECK (source IN ('typed', 'usda')),
    source_id TEXT
)

CREATE TABLE meals (
    id      TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    name    TEXT NOT NULL
)

CREATE TABLE meal_foods (
    id       TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    meal_id  TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES meals (id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    food_id  TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES foods (id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    quantity REAL NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0)
)

CREATE TABLE entries (
    id       TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id  TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    date     TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (strftime('%Y-%m-%d', date) IS date),
    section  TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (section IN ('breakfast', 'lunch', 'dinner', 'snacks')),
    food_id  TEXT REFERENCES foods (id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    meal_id  TEXT REFERENCES meals (id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    quantity REAL,
    CHECK ((food_id IS NOT NULL) + (meal_id IS NOT NULL) = 1),
    CHECK ((food_id IS NULL) = (quantity IS NULL)),
    CHECK (quantity IS NULL OR quantity > 0)
)
CREATE INDEX entries_by_user_date ON entries (user_id, date)

CREATE TABLE meta (
    key   TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    value TEXT NOT NULL
)

delete_policy.rule: Nothing cascades. Every reference is ON DELETE RESTRICT, so the database itself refuses to break a reference (R11).
delete_policy.why_both_layers: The refusal a person sees has to name what still uses the record ('used in 2 meals (Typical breakfast, Pasta night)'), which is a query, not an error message. So the API checks first and explains; the foreign key is the backstop that holds even if a route forgets to check.

reported_by.must_name: the meals that use it, and the dates that log it directly

delete_policy.note: The app removes an entry (that is an entry/remove, not a delete of a record), but no route deletes a user. Its references are RESTRICT anyway. There is no longer a day to delete: emptying a date is deleting its entries.

seed.when: Only when the database is empty - no rows in users. Checked before inserting anything, so a restart or a rebuild never re-seeds or duplicates.
seed.what: The same sample the frontend ships today: 31 foods, 5 meals, and 17 entries falling on 3 dates (today, yesterday, the day before), for the MVP user.
seed.whose: user 'user', the only account the MVP signs in to.
seed.source_of_truth: This moves to the backend, because the backend is what writes it. The frontend's lib/seed.ts stops being the source of the data and is retired in Part 7; the tests that compute expectations from it are re-pointed at the API then.
seed.dates: The three dates are relative to the date of first run, as they are now. They do not re-date themselves later, so the seeded history ages.

not_in_this_schema.why: Dropped on 2026-11-01, after the schema had been approved and built. A day of the log is the entries sharing a date, so a table holding it was a second home for the same fact - and a row that had to be created before anything could be logged into it, which is why an endpoint to open a day had to be invented in Part 6. With the date on the entry, logging any date works, a date with nothing on it reads as an empty day, and there is no 'no such day' to answer. What is given up: a stored empty day, and a place for facts about a day rather than about an entry. Neither is needed by any requirement; if one becomes needed, a small days(user_id, date) side table can hold it and be joined on the date, without touching entries.

not_in_this_schema.omitted: targets (2,200 kcal / 140 g protein / 250 g carbs / 70 g fat)
not_in_this_schema.why: R10 and R17 say one place, frontend/lib/targets.ts. Nothing stores them yet, and the API returns sums, not judgements, so the frontend keeps comparing against them.
Nothing reads them. Add them when something does.

One version, created if absent, and a meta row that names it. A file from an older version is migrated where a step exists for that version and refused where none does - a file this build cannot carry forward must not be read as if it matched. The first step exists: 2 -> 3, which rebuilds `foods` with the widened unit CHECK and copies every row across untouched (see docs/DATABASE.md). It was written because the gram basis arrived after the log was real, and 'delete the file' is not a migration.
The MVP credential is a constant in the application (R1), and the session lives in a signed cookie. Neither is data.

open_questions_for_sign_off: Answered 2026-11-01: TEXT ids everywhere, the meta row stays, the file lives at /data/nutrition.db in a named volume, and targets stay out of the database.
Should targets become per user later? Nothing in the schema stops it, and nothing in the schema does it.
